lectures.title: Mempool, MEV and DEX Trades - lesson synthesis
Mempool, MEV and DEX Trades - reading synthesis

questions.question_stem: Block 9: the transaction runs from Account 3 to the router, a cUSD Transfer runs from Account 3 to the pool, a WETH Transfer from the pool to Account 3, and Swap's sender is the router. Which sentence should the analyst give the agent?
questions.correct_answer: Account 3 sold 5,000 cUSD for WETH in the course pool, through the router; the other side was the pool, code and not a person.
incorrect_answers: The router sold 5,000 cUSD for WETH in the course pool, because it is the Swap sender and it called the pool for the trade.
Account 3 traded 5,000 cUSD with the router, which paid out the WETH from the reserves that it holds for the course pool.
Account 3 sold 5,000 cUSD to the pool's operator, who agreed to the price and then sent back the WETH from the pool.
questions.explanation: The input token's Transfer shows Account 3 sending cUSD, and the pool sends back the WETH, so Account 3 traded with a pool. Swap's sender is the router only because it called the pool; the router holds nothing and is not the seller.

questions.question_stem: In block 9's Swap log, amount0In is 5,000 and amount1Out is 2.3741. How does the analyst know that cUSD was the token sold?
questions.correct_answer: amount0 follows the pool's token0(), which returns cUSD here, so amount0In is the cUSD that went in.
incorrect_answers: amount1 is always the volatile token, so amount1Out is the WETH and amount0In is the cUSD.
The In amounts count what the trader receives, so the 5,000 is paid out by the pool and cUSD was bought.
Swap's amounts are the router's and name no token, so only the Transfer logs can say which was sold.
questions.explanation: In a Uniswap V2 pair, amount0 and amount1 follow the pool's token0() and token1(). Here token0() returns cUSD, so amount0In is the cUSD that went in, and amount1Out is the WETH paid out.

questions.question_stem: Account 3's swap, nonce 1, is stuck in the mempool. Its next transaction, nonce 2, offers a far higher tip. What happens?
questions.correct_answer: Nonce 2 cannot run first, whatever it pays: an account's transactions run in nonce order.
incorrect_answers: Nonce 2 runs first, because builders order all pending transactions by what each one pays them.
Nonce 2 replaces the stuck swap, because a higher fee cancels an earlier pending transaction.
Nonce 2 is dropped from the mempool, because a node holds one pending transaction per account.
questions.explanation: An account's transactions run in nonce order, so nonce 2 waits for nonce 1 whatever it pays. Only a transaction with the same nonce and a higher fee replaces a pending one.

questions.question_stem: Account 3 sends its swap to the public mempool. Who can read it before a block includes it?
questions.correct_answer: Anyone running a node, searchers' bots among them, because the mempool is public by default.
incorrect_answers: Only the block's builder, because pending trades go to builders and to nobody else in advance.
Only validators, because they alone hold the pending transactions for the next block.
Only the exchange's operator, because the DEX's contracts hold each order until a block takes it.
questions.explanation: The mempool is public by default, so anyone running a node can read a pending trade, including its minimum out. Searchers' bots do exactly that.
questions.lesson_block: Check: who sees the swap before it lands?

specific_source.reading: ethereum.org on transactions and on maximal extractable value: the mempool is public and pending transactions can be read

questions.question_stem: A sender sets maxFeePerGas to 50 gwei and maxPriorityFeePerGas to 2 gwei. The base fee is 30 gwei. What is charged, and where does it go?
questions.correct_answer: 32 gwei: the 30 gwei base fee is burned, the 2 gwei tip goes to the fee recipient, and 18 gwei is never charged.
incorrect_answers: 50 gwei: the sender pays the whole cap, and the 20 gwei above the base fee all goes to the tip as a bonus.
32 gwei: the 2 gwei tip is burned and the 30 gwei base fee goes to the proposer, with the rest refunded.
30 gwei: the base fee alone, because a tip is added only when blocks run above half of the block gas limit.
questions.explanation: The charge is the lower of the cap and base fee plus tip: 30 plus 2 is 32 gwei. The base fee is burned, the tip goes to the fee recipient, and the 18 gwei of headroom is never charged.
questions.lesson_block: Fees set the queue: base fee burned, tip paid

specific_source.reading: EIP-1559 (Buterin et al.): base fee burned, priority fee to the block's fee recipient, fee capped by the sender

questions.question_stem: A trainee says MEV is just the fee a validator earns for proposing a block. What is MEV, as the lesson defines it?
questions.correct_answer: Value taken from block production, beyond reward and fees, by including, leaving out or reordering transactions.
incorrect_answers: The reward and gas fees a validator earns for proposing a block, paid when it includes the transactions.
Value a miner extracts on proof-of-work chains only, a practice that ended once blocks moved to validators, who earn it.
The fee a searcher pays a builder to include a bundle, burned together with the block's base fee each slot.
questions.explanation: MEV is value extracted from block production beyond the reward and fees, by including, leaving out or reordering transactions. It is not the validator's ordinary reward.
questions.lesson_block: MEV is profit from choosing the order

specific_source.reading: MEV is profit from choosing the order

questions.question_stem: In lab block A a bot buys before the subject and sells after, and the subject got exactly its minimum. What does that minimum do in a sandwich?
questions.correct_answer: It caps the damage: the router refuses the trade if the output falls below it.
incorrect_answers: It hides the swap from the mempool, because a minimum above zero keeps it private.
It sets the bot's profit, because the bot keeps whatever the minimum leaves unspent.
It puts the subject first in the block, because a set minimum outranks a bot's tip.
questions.explanation: The minimum out is the trader's floor. If the bot pushes the output below it, the router refuses the trade, so the minimum caps the damage.

questions.question_stem: In the mainnet sandwich, a trader paid 220,806 USDC and got 5,273 USDT back, with a minimum of 0. What does the minimum of 0 show?
questions.correct_answer: There was no floor: the router accepted any price, so the bot could push the price freely.
incorrect_answers: The router would have refused the trade if the bot had not borrowed from Aave in its front-run.
The trader had chosen the price the bot would pay for the position just before the trade.
The builder keeps the trader's output whenever the minimum is 0, which was the loss.
questions.explanation: A minimum of 0 means no floor. The router accepted any price, so the bot could push the price as far as it liked and the trade still ran.

questions.question_stem: In the MEV-Boost chain, who picks the best bid and signs the header, and who keeps the block body hidden until then?
questions.correct_answer: The validator picks the best bid and signs the header; the relay keeps the body hidden until the header is signed.
incorrect_answers: The builder picks the best bid and signs the header; the searcher keeps the body hidden until it is signed.
The relay picks the best bid and signs the header; the validator keeps the body hidden until it is released.
The searcher picks the best bid and signs the header; the builder keeps the body hidden until signing it.
questions.explanation: Searchers send bundles to builders, builders build blocks, and relays pass only the header and bid. The validator picks the best bid and signs the header, and then the relay releases the block body.
questions.lesson_block: Searchers, builders and relays set the order

specific_source.reading: Flashbots docs: builders, relays and MEV-Boost; the relay hides the block body until the validator signs the header

questions.question_stem: Address 0xB07 buys token X in pool P just before the subject and sells X just after, and it trades in many other pools. Is it working with the subject?
questions.correct_answer: No: a sandwich bot, a third party; High confidence, because the pattern and its many pools are the evidence.
incorrect_answers: It traded on both sides of the subject in that block, so it is a second wallet; Moderate, pending its other pools.
Yes: sitting beside the subject in one block is a link; High, because that order cannot be chance.
Nothing can be said: a builder set the order, so the pattern is no evidence; Low, with the bot unknown.
questions.explanation: An address that trades before and after the subject, and in many unrelated pools, is a sandwich bot. Position next to a trade is not a link; the pattern across pools is the evidence, hence High.

questions.question_stem: Two wallets both sent swaps to the same 1inch router address. What does that show?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing about a link: many traders use the router, so it is a service in the path.
incorrect_answers: A link: both used one address, so they are one subject's wallets until shown otherwise.
That the wallets traded with each other, since the router is each trade's other party.
That each wallet paid 1inch a fee, so the two wallets are customers who work together.
questions.explanation: A router or aggregator such as 1inch is a service used by many traders. Two wallets that both used it are not linked by that.

specific_source.reading: Routers and aggregators are only in the path

questions.question_stem: A smart-account transaction was paid for by a paymaster. What does that make the paymaster?
questions.correct_answer: A service that paid for the operation, not the actor; the actor is the smart account.
incorrect_answers: The actor, because the party that pays for an operation is the party that made it.
The subject's partner, because it agreed in advance to fund that account's trades in full.
The bundler, because a paymaster is the contract that sends the transaction on.
questions.explanation: A paymaster covers the cost of a UserOperation. It is a service in the path; the actor is the smart account whose operation ran.
questions.lesson_block: Paymasters and relayers pay gas, not the bill

specific_source.reading: ERC-4337 account abstraction: bundlers, the EntryPoint and paymasters; a paymaster sponsors gas for an operation

questions.question_stem: A relayer sends a user's signed request, and the transaction's from is the relayer. Who is the real party?
questions.correct_answer: The signer, whose address is appended to the call data, not the relayer named in the from field.
incorrect_answers: The relayer, because it is the from of the transaction and it paid the gas for the request it forwarded.
The receiving contract, because it reads the call data and acts as the author of the request.
The paymaster, because it repays the relayer and so is the party behind the signed request.
questions.explanation: A gas relayer pays the gas and appears in the from field, but the signer's address is appended to the call data. The receiving contract reads the signer from there, so the signer is the real party.

questions.question_stem: The transaction's from is a bundler and its to is the EntryPoint; the two Transfer logs and Swap's to name a smart account. Who traded, and how sure?
questions.correct_answer: The smart account sold 2,000 cUSD for 0.98 WETH through the router; High, because the logs name it directly.
incorrect_answers: The bundler sold 2,000 cUSD for 0.98 WETH, because it signed the transaction; High, as it is the from.
The router sold 2,000 cUSD for 0.98 WETH, because Swap's sender names it; Moderate, as it is a service.
The smart account, but only Low confidence, because the chain cannot say who holds its signing key.
questions.explanation: The bundler only sent the UserOperation and paid gas. The Transfer logs and Swap name the smart account, a direct read of the logs, so High.

questions.question_stem: After reading the logs, the analyst knows the smart account traded. What can the chain not say about it?
questions.correct_answer: Who holds the key that signed the UserOperation; that is a question for other sources.
incorrect_answers: Whether the smart account made the trade, since only a pattern, not a log, names it.
Which address the WETH went to, since Swap's to is the router and not the final recipient.
What the bundler is, since a service in the from field cannot be told apart on chain.
questions.explanation: The logs establish which smart account traded. They cannot say who holds the key that signed the UserOperation; that needs other sources.

questions.question_stem: Which log names whose tokens were sold, and why is Swap's sender not the answer?
questions.correct_answer: The input Transfer's from; Swap's sender is the router, which called the pool.
incorrect_answers: Swap's sender, because the pool records whoever supplied the input as the sender.
Sync, because it records which account's tokens were added to the pool's reserves.
The output token's Transfer to, because the recipient is always the one who sold.
questions.explanation: The input token's Transfer from names whose tokens were sold. Swap's sender is the router, because the router called the pool.
